titel: Expected value, Kelly and the probability of ruin
kurz: Why the same strategy multiplies or destroys capital depending on position size, and where the limit lies mathematically.

bloecke.md:
Two traders trade the same signal. Both are right in 40% of cases and have a reward-to-risk ratio (RRR) of 1.8, so the expected value per trade is positive for both. One risks 1% of capital per position, the other 20%. After 1,000 trades, the first has tripled their money, while the second has around one fifty-thousandth of their starting capital left. The difference is due neither to discipline nor to bad luck; it follows from the arithmetic.

The expected value per trade is an **arithmetic mean**. It describes what comes out on average across many traders trading in parallel. Capital, however, grows multiplicatively and not additively, because each trade builds on the amount the previous one left. For the path of a single portfolio over time, the **geometric mean** is therefore what counts. At 20% risk per trade, the arithmetic expected value is +2.4%, and the geometric growth rate is −1.09%. Both figures are correct, but only the second describes how your own portfolio develops.

bloecke.formel: G(f) = p × ln(1 + b × f) + q × ln(1 − f)
bloecke.erklaerung: Expected logarithmic return per trade with a constant capital fraction f. The logarithm is the only function that turns multiplication into addition. Only with it can the individual trades be combined into a rate over time.
variablen: share of capital risked per trade

bloecke.titel: Two means of the same strategy
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation for p = 40% and RRR 1.8. The arithmetic expected value rises linearly with position size, while the geometric growth rate turns negative from 13.5%.

bloecke.md:
## The Kelly fraction

The gold growth-rate curve first rises, reaches a maximum and then falls. In 1956, John L. Kelly Jr. calculated where this maximum lies, in a paper on communication channels, not on stock exchanges. The fraction that maximises the long-term growth rate has been called the Kelly fraction ever since.

bloecke.erklaerung: The growth-optimal share of capital per trade. If the numerator is negative, the strategy has a negative expected value, and then any position size is too large.

bloecke.titel: Position size, expected value and final capital (illustrative calculation, p = 40%, RRR 1.8, excluding costs and taxes)

bloecke.md:
The table shows three relationships that are not obvious.

First, the curve is flat to the left of the optimum and steep to the right of it. At 1% risk instead of the optimal 6.7%, you still achieve just over a quarter of the possible growth rate. At 20% risk, you lose money with the same signal. So a stake that is too small costs return, while one that is too large can cost the entire account.

Second, the point at which growth falls to zero lies at roughly twice the Kelly fraction. This applies in general and not only to these parameters. In the continuous-time approximation, the growth rate at a multiple c of the Kelly fraction is exactly (2c − c²) times the maximum. For c = 2, this gives zero.

Third, this gives rise to the symmetry that has made half Kelly the standard. For c = 0.5, the result is 2 × 0.5 − 0.25 = 0.75, that is, 75% of the maximum growth rate at half the volatility.

A positive expected value per trade does not guarantee growth. From twice the Kelly fraction, capital no longer grows despite a positive expectation, and above that it shrinks with certainty. Position size alone can turn a working strategy into a losing one without anything about the strategy changing.

## Ruin with fractional betting

With constant fractional betting, the capital can mathematically never reach exactly zero, because only a fraction is ever staked. In practice, this is irrelevant. The capital can very well fall below any threshold at which minimum order sizes, margin requirements or your own nerves set a limit. What matters, therefore, is the probability of falling at some point to a fraction a of the starting capital, and not the probability of reaching zero euros.

bloecke.formel: P(capital reaches fraction a at some point) = a^(2/c − 1)
bloecke.erklaerung: Continuous-time approximation (geometric Brownian motion) for constant fractional betting. The formula applies to the entire future, not to a limited period. The decline is counted whenever it occurs, not only if it happens immediately.
variablen: fraction of the starting capital, e.g. 0.5 for a halving
multiple of the Kelly fraction staked
bloecke.beispiel: At full Kelly (c = 1), the exponent is 2/1 − 1 = 1, so P = a. The probability of losing half the capital at some point is therefore exactly 50% at full Kelly.

bloecke.titel: Probability of falling below a threshold at some point
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation using P = a^(2/c − 1). At full Kelly, the probability of a halving is 50% and that of losing four fifths of the capital is 20%, in each case measured against the starting capital. A decline of this size from an interim peak, by contrast, will occur with certainty at some point if trading continues long enough.

bloecke.titel: Estimation errors in p and b
bloecke.md: The Kelly formula assumes that the win rate and the reward-to-risk ratio are known. In a backtest, this is never the case. Both values are estimates from a sample, usually from the same price history on which the rule was developed. If the win rate is assumed to be 45% instead of 40%, the result is a Kelly fraction of 14.4%. The true zero-growth point, however, is 13.5%. An estimate that is five percentage points too optimistic is therefore enough to turn a strategy that would have multiplied capital 51.2 times with the correct Kelly fraction of 6.7% into one that leaves just a third after 1,000 trades. The formula thus reacts asymmetrically to estimation errors. Underestimation costs return; overestimation costs capital.

The signal provides for an entry at €50 and a stop at €47, so the risk per unit is €3. The win rate is 40%, and the RRR is 1.8.

- Full Kelly (6.67%) means €1,667 of risk, 555 units and a nominal volume of €27,750. That is 111% of the portfolio value. Kelly would be uncomfortable here and cannot be implemented without leverage anyway.
- Half Kelly (3.33%) means €833 of risk, 277 units and a nominal volume of €13,850, that is, 55% of the portfolio in a single position.
- At 1% risk, it is €250 of risk, 83 units and a nominal volume of €4,150.

With tight stops, even half Kelly usually leads to a concentrated position. The formula provides a risk share and not a capital commitment, and it only ever considers one trade. With three correlated positions held at the same time, three times the fraction is effectively staked.

bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with a lognormal approximation of the capital path (p = 40%, RRR 1.8, excluding costs and taxes). The band runs from the 10th to the 90th percentile, and the line shows the median. Even with a genuine edge, it takes around 250 trades until the bottom tenth is back in positive territory.

bloecke.md:
The dispersion of this fan is the main reason for fractional Kelly. Even a genuine edge only shows itself after hundreds of trades and not in a feeling of success. Until then, a path in the bottom tenth looks exactly like that of a strategy with no edge at all. With 60% losing trades, at least one streak of five consecutive losses occurs within 100 trades with a probability of 97.6%. Switching strategy because of such a streak is a reaction to chance. Increasing position sizes instead shortens the road to ruin.

This yields the order of priority in which survival comes before return. Return is an average across many paths; survival is a property of the one path an investor actually goes through. A path that has been cut off no longer enters any average. That is why ruin cannot be made up for by later gains, whereas forgoing some return can.

## Costs and taxes

All the figures so far have been calculated without trading costs and taxes. Capital income is subject to 25% flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) under Section 32d(1) EStG (Income Tax Act) plus 5.5% solidarity surcharge, together 26.375%. With church tax, it is around 27.8% to 28.0%. The saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000, or €2,000 for joint assessment (Section 20(9) EStG), is used up after a few weeks of active trading.

As a simplification, the tax of 26.375% can be treated as an ongoing charge on every winning trade, with losses in the same year offset against it. The growth rate at 1% risk then falls from 0.111% to 0.083% per trade, and the 3.0-fold result after 1,000 trades becomes 2.3-fold. The tax rate is 26.4%, but only around 64% of the increase remains, because the tax paid away no longer compounds.

This simplification is still optimistic. Losses only reduce the tax via the bank's loss offset pots (Verlustverrechnungstöpfe), and not at the moment they arise. Two restrictions apply to these pots. Losses from share sales may only be offset against gains from share sales (Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG), and whatever remains open at the end of the year is carried forward without interest. For derivative transactions (Termingeschäfte), the former cap of €20,000 a year no longer applies. The Annual Tax Act 2024 (Jahressteuergesetz) abolished it without replacement, applicable in all open cases (Section 52(28) EStG). For share losses, the special pot remains.

Tax and trading costs reduce the edge and therefore also f*. Trading costs are more damaging than tax, because they are also incurred on losing trades. With total costs of 0.10% per round turn on the nominal volume, the costs of 250 round turns a year add up to 25 percentage points if each round turn moves the entire capital. Because the costs of each round turn are deducted from the capital remaining at the time, the capital at the end of the year is around 22% lower than without these costs. That is more than most edges earn. For the position with 1% risk from the example, each round turn moves only €4,150, around one sixth of the portfolio. The capital is then around 4% lower.

Practitioners stake a quarter to a half of the Kelly fraction. There are four reasons for this, which work together:

1. Estimation errors arise because p and b come from finite samples. Fractional Kelly keeps a safety margin from the zero-growth point.
2. An edge that existed from 2019 to 2023 need not still exist in 2026 (**non-stationarity**). The formula, by contrast, assumes constant parameters.
3. Several simultaneous positions in the same sector are, because of their correlation, one trade and not three.
4. Under full Kelly, a drawdown of 50% is the normal case and not an exception. Investors who get out at that point realise the bad half of the distribution and miss the good one.

According to the summary by MacLean, Thorp and Ziemba (2010), Kelly is asymptotically optimal, but the path to get there is intolerable for most users.

Three quantities are of practical use: the zero-growth point at roughly 2 × f*, which is suitable as a hard upper limit; your own f, measured as the total share at risk across all open positions; and the question of how far p may fall before your own f is above 2 × f*. With these three figures, the formula is rarely needed afterwards.

mitnehmen: The expected value per trade is an average across many traders, whereas the development of your own portfolio is described by the geometric growth rate.
The growth-optimal share of capital is f* = (b × p − q) / b; at twice that share, the growth rate is zero, and above it negative, even though the expectation per trade is positive.
Under full Kelly, the probability of losing half the capital at some point is 50%; under half Kelly, it is 12.5%, with 75% of the growth rate still retained.
Kelly reacts asymmetrically to estimation errors: a win rate set just five percentage points too high is enough to exceed the zero-growth point.

Taxes (25% flat-rate withholding tax under Section 32d(1) EStG and solidarity surcharge under Section 4 SolzG 1995 (Solidarity Surcharge Act), together 26.375%) and trading costs reduce the edge and therefore the permissible position size, with costs being incurred on losing trades as well.

begriffe.text: The share of capital f* = (b × p − q) / b that maximises the long-term geometric growth rate. The criterion assumes that the probability of a win p and the reward-to-risk ratio b are known.

The rate at which a single pool of capital grows over time, calculated via the logarithm of the period factors. It is always below the arithmetic expected value, and the difference grows with volatility.
Stake above the Kelly fraction. From twice f* upwards, the growth rate is zero or negative, even though the expected value per trade remains positive.

Deliberately staking a fraction c of the Kelly fraction. The growth rate is then (2c − c²) times the maximum, and the probability of a decline to the fraction a of the capital is a to the power of (2/c − 1).

With fractional betting, the probability of falling below a set capital threshold at some point. This does not mean the probability of exactly zero euros, because with this approach the capital never reaches that value.
